item.title: 🔵 Claude, Copilot and Agentforce are ready. Are your SAP and ServiceNow platforms ready?
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

At a 2027 planning session in October, I watched a leadership team approve three AI agent pilots in under ten minutes. The three were a claims-intake agent, a collections agent and a finance close assistant, each with a sponsor, a vendor quote and a slide of projected savings. The next item on the agenda was the SAP clean-core program those same agents would run on. It took forty minutes, drew questions about payback and slipped to 2028.

Nobody in the room did anything wrong. The agents came in as an operating expense from the innovation fund and were judged on speed to value. The clean-core program came in as a capital project and was judged on a three-year payback—two committees, two tests, one dependency that neither test could see. The agents were funded. The platform they would run on was not.

Versions of that meeting play out in most of the programs I advise, from banks to state Medicaid agencies. It is the planning mistake I see most often this budget season, and you can fix it before January.

item.title: 🔵 What developers and QA need from each other when AI writes the code
item.description:

The change was a small edit to a shared component. It passed code review and QA; the tests were green and the code did what the ticket asked.

When a customer purchased a subscription and closed the browser, the system normally turned that order into working access in the background. The change, however, broke that step. An alert from the live system’s logs caught the failure that QA and the code reviewers did not.

The tests weren’t what failed. The handoff was. No one had documented which other services used that component, or in what order they had to change.

Developers’ work and QA’s work come together at the handoff. AI strains that handoff by multiplying changes like this one: small edits to shared code, arriving faster than anyone documents their dependencies.

item.title: 🟠 AI is changing the build-versus-buy equation. Are CIOs ready?
item.description:

For decades, CIOs have faced a familiar decision when evaluating enterprise software: Should we build it ourselves or buy it from a software provider?

The answer has often favored buying. Commercial software, particularly software as a service (SaaS), provides mature capabilities, ongoing enhancements and technical support. Building custom applications typically requires significant investments in developers, infrastructure, testing, security and maintenance.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to challenge that equation. With AI-powered development tools, applications that once required weeks or months of programming can sometimes be prototyped in hours or days. Developers can generate code, build interfaces and automate testing with less manual effort. Even employees with limited programming experience can describe what they want an application to do and have AI generate a working solution.

item.title: 🔵 The leadership gap when technical specialists become executives
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

A successful technical career can prepare someone to lead a function without preparing them to lead everything that comes next. Executive work brings distinct disciplines into the foreground: strategy, interpersonal leadership, business management, consulting and financial judgment. Technical expertise remains valuable, but these capabilities do not emerge automatically from it. They need deliberate development before promotion, not an assumption that the new title will produce them.

Consider a hypothetical programming lead who has spent 30 years writing code and guiding junior developers. That experience can produce excellent technical judgment and valuable mentoring skills. It does not, by itself, demonstrate an ability to choose a business strategy, allocate capital across functions or resolve competing organizational interests. The executive role is not simply the same programming job with more authority. It requires different kinds of judgment.

item.description:

The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them.

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide.

A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required.

There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets.
